analysis.one_liner: Requires employer health plans to cover mental illness on the same terms as physical illness.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan mental health parity bill with 69 Senate cosponsors died without ever getting a vote in the Senate committee it was assigned to.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employer group health plans that cover both physical and mental illness to apply the same deductibles, copays, and limits on visits to mental health care as to physical care. Plans would not have been forced to offer mental health benefits, and small employers with 50 or fewer employees were exempt. The bill was introduced by a senior Republican, gathered 69 cosponsors from both parties, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in the Senate Health Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families in large employer health plans who face higher copays, stricter visit limits, and annual or lifetime caps on mental health care than on physical care. Insured people treated for depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and other DSM-diagnosed conditions would have gotten comparable cost-sharing and treatment limits.

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans from imposing any treatment limitation or financial requirement on mental health benefits unless comparable limits apply to medical and surgical benefits, including deductibles, coinsurance, copays, and annual and lifetime limits [S3].
The rules apply separately to each benefit option a plan offers and to both self-insured plans under ERISA and insured group plans under the Public Health Service Act [S3].
The bill leaves stronger state parity laws in place rather than preempting them [S3].

It requires a government study of the rules' effects on insurance costs, access, and quality, and of the cost of extending the same parity to substance abuse treatment, which the bill itself excludes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers offering large group health plans and the insurers administering them, through higher expected claims when mental health cost-sharing and visit limits must match physical care. Employers with 2 to 50 employees are exempt, and plans can avoid the mandate entirely by dropping mental health benefits.

drawbacks.text: The bill would likely raise health insurance premiums for large employers, and some of that cost could reach workers through lower wages or reduced benefits [S3].
Plans were not required to offer mental health benefits at all, so an employer could comply by dropping mental health coverage rather than putting it on par [S3].
Substance abuse and chemical dependency treatment were excluded from parity, despite being among the largest coverage gaps, pending a future cost study [S3].
Out-of-network mental health benefits did not have to meet parity as long as in-network benefits did and the plan provided reasonable access to in-network providers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For millions of insured workers with serious mental illness, the bill would have removed the practice of charging them higher copays and capping their treatment days far below what physical illness gets. The costs were real but targeted: large employers and insurers bore higher expected claims, while small employers were exempt and plans kept broad tools to manage care. The strongest honest criticism is the loopholes — no requirement to offer mental health benefits at all, no substance abuse parity, and no out-of-network parity — which narrowed who was protected.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor; it died there when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Pete Domenici (R-NM) introduced the bill on February 27, 2003, with 25 original cosponsors from both parties [S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
A total of 69 senators — 47 Democrats, 21 Republicans, and 1 Independent — signed on as cosponsors, a majority of the chamber [S4].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers and health insurers, who avoided a mandate to equalize mental health cost-sharing and treatment limits, and the committee leadership that never took the bill up.

for.name: Pete Domenici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push, naming it for his late Minnesota colleague Paul Wellstone.

for.name: Ted Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor and longtime champion of mental health parity legislation.

for.name: 69 of 100 Senators
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, 47 Democrats, 21 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

against.name: Judd Gregg
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill received no action after referral and died there.

against.name: Employer coalitions and health insurance industry
against.role: Business groups representing large employers and insurers, including the ERISA Industry Committee and National Association of Health Underwriters
against.what_they_did: Opposed parity mandates, arguing they would drive up health premiums and could push employers to drop mental health coverage; such campaigns never appear in the congressional record but were widely reported at the time.

sides.party_line_note: Support was strongly bipartisan: the sponsor was a senior Republican, 21 of the 69 cosponsors were Republicans, and the original cosponsors included Grassley, Warner, Specter, Collins, and Chafee alongside Kennedy, Daschle, and Reid [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Large employers offering group health plans
industries.note: The bill would have required plans covering 51 or more employees to match mental health cost-sharing and visit limits to physical care, raising expected claims costs. Small employers were exempt. Employer groups opposed parity mandates on cost grounds; the bill's death spared them the expense.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care companies
industries.note: Insurers would have had to pay mental health claims on the same terms as physical claims, cutting into savings from strict mental health limits. The bill preserved their ability to manage care through preauthorization and utilization review, and left them free to drop mental health coverage entirely.
Therapists, psychiatrists, and clinics would have seen far more covered visits as plan-imposed day and visit caps had to match physical care limits, expanding access for their patients.
